nameStory: This tiny green algae gets its scientific name from the Greek 'tetra' meaning four and 'desmus' meaning chain or bond, referring to how it typically forms colonies of four cells linked together. The species name 'obliquus' means slanted or oblique in Latin, describing the slightly asymmetrical, tilted shape of its spindle-like cells.
description: Tetradesmus obliquus is a microscopic green algae that lives in freshwater throughout New England. You won't see individual cells without a microscope - they're only about the width of a human hair! This algae forms small colonies of 2-4 cells arranged in a single row, though sometimes you'll find solitary cells floating freely. Each cell is spindle-shaped with pointed ends and contains a bright green chloroplast that fills the entire cell.

idTips.label: Colony formation
idTips.description: Look for groups of 2-4 spindle-shaped cells arranged in a straight line under the microscope, though single cells are common too

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are spindle-shaped like tiny green footballs, tapering to sharp points at both ends

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Cells are extremely small, typically 6-15 micrometers long - you'd need to line up about 10 cells to equal the width of a human hair

idTips.label: Chloroplast
idTips.description: Each cell contains a single bright green chloroplast that fills the entire cell, with a small round structure (pyrenoid) visible in the center

idTips.label: Asymmetry
idTips.description: Cells often appear slightly lopsided or tilted rather than perfectly symmetrical, giving them a characteristic oblique appearance

habitat: You'll find this microscopic algae in virtually any freshwater habitat across New England - from pristine mountain ponds to urban retention basins, quiet stream backwaters, and even temporary puddles. It thrives in both clean and nutrient-rich waters, making it one of our most adaptable aquatic microorganisms. Look for it in pond samples, especially where there's some organic matter or gentle water movement.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing actively as waters warm and daylight increases. Best time to find robust colonies in pond samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with abundant populations in most freshwater bodies. Colonies are most active and easiest to observe.
seasonality.fall: Still present and active in warmer waters, though populations may decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Populations persist under ice in deeper waters, though growth slows significantly. May be dormant in shallow or temporary water bodies.

funFact: This tiny algae is being studied as a potential solution to our plastic pollution problem - scientists have discovered that microscopic plastic particles actually affect how well it can photosynthesize, making it a living detector for plastic contamination in our waterways!
confusionNotes: This species was formerly known as Scenedesmus obliquus, so you'll often see it listed under that name in older field guides and scientific papers. Under the microscope, it can be confused with other small green algae, but the combination of spindle-shaped cells in small linear colonies is distinctive.
contextualKnowledge: Like many microscopic organisms, this species has undergone recent name changes as DNA studies have revealed new relationships. What scientists called Scenedesmus obliquus for decades is now properly known as Tetradesmus obliquus, though you'll still see both names used interchangeably in current literature.
compareHints: Tetradesmus obliquus forms smaller colonies (2-4 cells) compared to its relative T. lagerheimii, and its cells have the characteristic oblique or slightly asymmetrical shape that gives it its name. While both species form linear colonies, obliquus has more consistently spindle-shaped cells with sharper, more tapered ends than other members of the Scenedesmaceae family.
